overview: The atlas’s “Uyghurs” record compresses three different stories into 700-1000: Uyghur groups before imperial rule, the powerful Orkhon-based Uyghur Khaganate of 744-840, and successor communities centered farther south and west after its fall. Its polygons are especially misleading. The 700 shape misses the later capital; the 900 shape still surrounds ruined Ordu-Baliq while excluding tested points for Qocho/Turfan, Ganzhou and Beshbalik. Read the map as a rough locator, never as an exact border or a claim that one ethnic group filled every colored space. The khaganate connected mobile herding, a monumental city, Silk Road commerce, Tang diplomacy and multilingual writing. In 840, political conflict, animal losses, hunger, epidemic and Kyrgyz attack ended that empire. Uyghur people, families, scripts, religions, art and new states continued. This card separates those eras and marks what evidence cannot tell us about ordinary homes, schooling, medicine and toilets.

periods.title: Before the khaganate: an atlas label too early
periods.summary: Uyghur groups were part of a changing steppe world, but the empire conventionally dated 744-840 did not yet exist. The atlas’s 700 polygon lies far south and west of the later Orkhon capital.

periods.title: Coalition against the Eastern Türk rulers
periods.summary: Uyghur, Karluk and Basmil forces helped break Eastern Türk power; the Uyghur leader then defeated his partners and claimed the qaghan title in 744.

periods.title: A new khaganate and an Orkhon capital
periods.summary: The new ruling house established an empire centered in Mongolia and developed Ordu-Baliq, also called Karabalghasun, as a fortified political and commercial center.

periods.title: Tang alliance during the An Lushan rebellion
periods.summary: Uyghur armies assisted the Tang court against rebels. Military bargaining, silk payments, horses and a royal marriage made the alliance valuable and tense.

periods.title: Bögü Qaghan and Manichaean court patronage
periods.summary: After contact with Manichaean clergy, Bögü adopted their religion around 762/763 and supported it at court. That choice did not turn every subject into a Manichaean.

periods.title: Coup, contested policy and unstable succession
periods.summary: Bögü was killed in a 779 coup led by his cousin. Court conflict changed religious and foreign policy, and several short reigns followed.

periods.title: A restored dynasty, trade and a trilingual monument
periods.summary: A new ruling line restored stability after 795. The Karabalgasun inscription displayed authority in Old Turkic, Sogdian and Chinese while court trade and diplomacy revived.

periods.title: Marriage diplomacy, treaty and a compound crisis
periods.summary: Princess Taihe’s 821 marriage and the 822/823 Tibetan treaty marked high diplomacy. Later factional conflict, livestock disaster, epidemic, hunger and Kyrgyz attack combined in the destruction of the capital in 840.

periods.title: Successor Uyghur communities at Qocho and Ganzhou
periods.summary: The Mongolian khaganate ended, but refugees and established communities formed new centers in the Gansu corridor and Turpan region. The atlas keeps the old Mongolian shape instead of following those successors.

sections.title: First, fix the map in your head

items.text: The exact atlas target is id “uyghurs,” dated approximately 700 to 1000. That range is broader than the Uyghur Khaganate of 744 to 840. This card therefore begins with pre-imperial politics and ends with successor Uyghur communities; it does not pretend one government ruled for three centuries.

The 700 shape is especially unreliable. Its ten-point polygon sits south and west of the later imperial heartland and contains none of the tested locations for Ordu-Baliq, Turfan, Ganzhou or Beshbalik. Treat it as a misplaced label, not a border that a medieval customs officer could patrol.

The 800 shape finally contains Ordu-Baliq in Mongolia, but it stretches extraordinarily far east and still misses later oasis centers. It can help you find the empire’s core on a globe. It cannot tell you which pasture, market, caravan or neighboring community obeyed the qaghan on a particular day.

The 900 shape creates the opposite historical problem: it still wraps around the ruined Mongolian capital while excluding tested points for Turfan, Ganzhou and Beshbalik, where successor histories belong. In short, the colored blob did not get the memo about 840.

Nearby records are separate stories. The atlas also has Göktürk, Western Göktürk, Karluk, Karakhanid and Xixia ids. Alliances, migration and reused titles connect them, but connection is not identity. No card is being shared across those records, and the 1000 cutoff is merely where this imported Uyghur label stops.

sections.title: From coalition to Silk Road superpower

items.text: In 742, Uyghur leaders joined Karluk and Basmil forces against the Eastern Türk rulers. The alliance did not stay equal for long: the Uyghur leader overcame his former partners and claimed the qaghan title in 744. Empire-building here looked less like drawing a fresh country and more like winning a dangerous coalition argument.

Ordu-Baliq, also called Karabalghasun, made imperial power visible. Its name joins ideas of a royal camp and a town, a useful reminder that rulers with mobile pastoral traditions could also sponsor walls, offices, workshops and markets. Steppe and city were partners, not opposite settings in a civilization quiz.

When the An Lushan rebellion shook Tang China after 755, Uyghur cavalry helped the Tang court recover its capitals. The alliance brought silk, status, trade and marriage links, but Chinese court historians also complained about costs and behavior. Allies can be grateful, suspicious and busy calculating the invoice all at once.

Bögü Qaghan adopted Manichaeism around 762/763 and protected its clergy. In 779 his cousin killed him in a coup; later rulers again supported the religion. Those turns show court policy, not a population-wide switch. The checked evidence cannot count what every household believed simply because a ruler chose new teachers.

After a new dynasty stabilized the court in 795, trade revived. Records for 829 and 830 describe thousands of horses exchanged for a combined 230,000 pieces of silk. The numbers come from political texts and may reflect bargaining as much as accounting, but they show the scale imagined for steppe-Tang exchange.

sections.title: Capital life: walls, markets and a thirteen-meter well

items.text: Karabalgasun spread far beyond one palace enclosure. Archaeology reveals workshops, domestic compounds and markets linked to roads, fields and surrounding pastoral country. Residents and visitors included Uyghurs, Chinese and Sogdians. Excavated rooms do not define one standard home, and “city” did not mean everyone abandoned seasonal movement.

The citadel stood on an artificial platform about ten meters high. Excavators identified gates, a paved courtyard, smaller buildings and a tower-like central structure; carved granite, gilded pieces, jade texts and a bronze bell hint at ceremony and administration. A dramatic platform impresses, though climbing it probably impressed your knees too.

A newly published study describes the citadel well as about thirteen meters deep, with stone lining and wooden casing. Ceramic vessels could scoop water; jade decree fragments and a gyrfalcon skeleton later entered the fill. Archaeologists study layers, so finding a falcon in a well does not mean falcon-flavored water was on the menu.

Animal bones and isotope evidence show several provisioning systems. Some livestock grazed nearby, some farther away, and some animals were tethered; meat and milk linked herders with urban households. Elite compounds may have drawn on their own herds. These samples reveal economic networks, not everybody’s favorite dinner.

The Orkhon valley offered water and pasture, while the capital acted as a military, administrative, commercial and religious hub. Markets and fixed buildings existed inside a landscape still shaped by mobile life. A family might depend on a city without sleeping behind its walls every night of the year.

sections.title: Families, children, meals, clothes and work

items.text: Princess Taihe married the Uyghur qaghan in 821 after lengthy negotiations and traveled with a very large escort. A Tang record calls her qatun, or khatun. This was geopolitics performed as a wedding, not a typical family party, and it tells us almost nothing about how most couples chose partners or divided chores.

A funerary banner from tenth- to eleventh-century Qocho says Kara Totok’s son commissioned it for him. That tiny statement makes grief and family duty visible, although the honored man was high-ranking and the object reaches slightly beyond the atlas endpoint. Ordinary families left fewer named monuments.

A painted scene from the wider Uyghur oasis world shows monks receiving instruction, and manuscript collections preserve dictionaries and grammatical lists. They prove organized religious learning and language study. They do not give us school-enrollment rates, the age when most children started, or enough evidence to claim that girls and boys had equal access.

At medieval Turpan, archaeobotanical finds include grapes, millet, wheat and barley. At the capital, animal evidence points to meat and dairy production. Recipes, incomes and beliefs varied, and the crop study runs from the ninth to thirteenth centuries, so this is a pantry of possibilities rather than one official Uyghur breakfast.

Qocho paintings show some Manichaean clerics in white robes and other figures in regionally recognizable riding clothes. Documents mention taxes, labor duties, property and travel permits. Clothing could signal occupation or status, while work ranged from herding and farming to craft, trade, administration and religious service. Many surviving documents are later than 1000, so no one costume or job fits everyone in this card.

sections.title: Belief, books and a written Uyghur name

items.text: The Karabalgasun monument carried texts in Old Turkic runiform, Sogdian and Chinese. That trilingual choice made one ruler’s message legible to different political and trading audiences. Large damaged portions prevent a complete reading, but the stone remains an achievement in multilingual public communication.

A small authentic sample from the Suji inscription is 𐰆𐰖𐰍𐰆𐰺, transliterated Uyγur and meaning “Uyghur.” It is an ethnonym, not a whole sentence. Old Turkic runiform lines were normally read from right to left, so the direction may feel backward to readers used to English.

Old Uyghur script is a different writing system from the runiform sample. It developed from cursive Sogdian in the eighth to ninth centuries and was used extensively in the oasis kingdoms, often in vertical lines. It was later adapted for Mongolian writing, giving a scribal experiment a very long afterlife.

Manichaean sponsorship encouraged carefully made books, calligraphy and painting. At Qocho, Buddhism also became increasingly important, while other beliefs remained present in the region. A ruler’s religion influenced institutions and art, but people’s private convictions are much harder to count than temples or manuscript fragments.

Berlin now holds thousands of Uighur manuscript fragments from Turfan. They preserve law, medicine, religion, language and ordinary transactions, but many arrived through early twentieth-century European expeditions and were split among collections. Reading the pages also means asking who removed them, how they were divided and whose heritage they represent.

sections.title: Medicine, water and the honest toilet answer

items.text: Old Uyghur medical fragments name plants, animal and mineral ingredients, ailments and attempted treatments. Scholars find influences from Syriac, Indian, Chinese and local traditions. Most surviving manuscripts are not securely confined to 700-1000, so they show a Uyghur medical literature, not a guaranteed khaganate-era prescription cabinet.

A treatment written down is evidence that someone recommended or copied it; it is not proof that the remedy worked. The checked sources do not establish public hospitals, licensed doctors or equal access to care. People probably relied on household knowledge, specialists and religious settings in varying combinations, but exact proportions are unknown.

At Ordu-Baliq, the citadel’s deep engineered well supplied an elite compound or official center. Its wooden casing, stone lining and water vessels demonstrate serious hydraulic work. One monumental well cannot tell us how every household fetched water, whether water stayed safe, or how many people shared each source.

Around Qocho, underground karez channels carried groundwater toward fields and settlements; nearby Yar used deep wells. Such systems helped oasis farming survive in a dry landscape. They required knowledge and maintenance, but UNESCO’s description does not show that every home had a private tap, bath or sewer.

So, what about toilets? The sources checked here document wells, channels, vessels and drains in the wider built landscape, but no household-latrine survey and no universal sewer network. The truthful answer is “we do not yet know enough.” Archaeology has found a thirteen-meter well and even a falcon in it, but no royal bathroom instruction manual.

sections.title: The fall of an empire and lives after 840

items.text: The winter of 839/840 brought severe cold and livestock losses amid epidemic, hunger and court conflict. Kyrgyz forces then attacked, killed the qaghan and destroyed the capital. Researchers caution that neither drought nor climate alone “caused” the collapse; environmental shock became deadly through political and military weakness.

The year 840 ended the Mongolian khaganate, not the Uyghur people. Some groups moved southwest or into the Gansu corridor; others joined communities already tied to oasis routes. “They disappeared” would erase refugees, survivors, local hosts and the new political experiments that followed defeat.

Qocho in the Turpan basin became a durable center of farming, trade, translation, art and several religions. A separate Uyghur polity developed around Ganzhou. These states were not the old empire teleported south: their environments, neighbors and institutions changed, even while rulers and communities carried Uyghur names and traditions.

Successor artists and scribes produced murals, banners and manuscripts in multiple languages and scripts. The shift from Old Turkic runiform to Old Uyghur writing, and that script’s later influence on Mongolian, show continuity through adaptation. Cultural survival is rarely a museum freeze-frame; it keeps borrowing tools.

The atlas drops the uyghurs id at 1000, yet neither people nor cultural traditions ended then. Old Uyghur writing remained in use for centuries and was later adapted for Mongolian. The imported map has simply reached its chosen boundary; its endpoint cannot erase the long documentary life visible beyond it.

ending.text: Kyrgyz attack and a compound political, economic and environmental crisis destroyed the Orkhon khaganate in 840. That date ends an imperial government, not a people. Uyghur groups moved into the Gansu corridor and oasis regions, where Qocho and Ganzhou became distinct successor centers; others followed different paths. The atlas’s 900 polygon wrongly keeps the old Mongolian core, and its 1000 endpoint is only a dataset cutoff. Languages, writing, art, belief, trade, agriculture and family life continued under changed states.
